description: The protected kernel. These rules are blocking from day one — unlike every other policy group, which starts advisory and is promoted only after demonstrated accuracy. The asymmetry is deliberate: a governance system that can silently rewrite the rules that judge it is not a governance system. No automation may weaken a rule here, broaden an MCP permission, accept a security exception, or approve its own governance change.

rules.statement: Every committed governance document validates against its JSON Schema.
rules.rationale: A malformed document is indistinguishable from a document that means something different. Schema validity is the floor everything else stands on.

rules.statement: Files listed in the generated-file registry reproduce byte-identically from their sources.
rules.rationale: A hand edit to a generated file is indistinguishable from staleness, and both mean the same thing: the committed bytes no longer follow from the sources. Regeneration comparison catches either.

rules.statement: Two consecutive syncs with no source change produce byte-identical output.
rules.rationale: Non-deterministic generation makes drift detection meaningless: every run would report a diff, and real drift would be lost in the noise. This is kernel scope and was never deferred.

rules.statement: No governance artifact contains a credential value, a connection URL query string, or userinfo.
rules.rationale: Governance reads the whole repository, so anything it writes is a potential exfiltration path. Names and classifications are always sufficient; values never are.

rules.statement: Sync never writes to a curated document, and the merge never silently discards curated intent.
rules.rationale: Generated files may be replaced deterministically; human intent may not. A merge conflict is surfaced as a finding rather than resolved by overwriting one side.

rules.statement: Every validator reference resolves to an ID in governance/validators.json, and no annotation or manifest carries executable shell text.
rules.rationale: Free-form validation strings let an annotation introduce a command — including a destructive env-gated suite that an agent following 'run the required validation' could be induced to enable. IDs through a reviewed registry make that structurally impossible.

rules.statement: Validators that mutate live services or send real messages stay out of the registry and are recorded in its excluded list.
rules.rationale: Selection must never be able to reach them. Being absent from the registry is the enforcement; the excluded list exists so the omission is explained rather than looking like an oversight.

rules.statement: A change touching governance/ or tools/repo_governance/ has a corresponding change record.
rules.rationale: The system that demands change records for the application must demand them of itself first. Everything outside governance/ is advisory until the process is proven.

rules.statement: The governance tool never imports app.* in-process; code that must execute application modules runs in a scrubbed subprocess.
rules.rationale: Settings loading walks parent directories for .env and main.py configures Logfire at import scope, so an in-process import can load real secrets and emit telemetry from a tool that is only supposed to read files.

rules.statement: Runtime-derived records stay under .cache/repo-governance/; committed artifacts reference evidence only by ID and summary.
rules.rationale: Runtime evidence is environment-specific and can contain tenant data or live credentials. Referencing it by ID keeps the finding auditable without moving the data.

rules.statement: Lowering a rule's maturity, or removing a rule, requires a change record naming the rule and its justification.
rules.rationale: Weakening a policy is the one change most likely to be made under deadline pressure and least likely to be noticed. Making it explicit is the whole point of self-governance.

rules.statement: The tool refuses to interpret a governance contract whose version it does not support.
rules.rationale: Interpreting a newer manifest as though it were valid is worse than failing: it produces confident, wrong answers.
